title: Subject-To Existing Financing Addendum
summary: An original addendum for buying a property subject to the seller's existing mortgage, with separately initialed acknowledgments by buyer and seller.
useWhen: Attach to a purchase contract when the buyer takes title while the seller's mortgage stays in place and the buyer makes the payments. Use with the Seller Acknowledgments and Disclosures.
watchOuts: Due-on-sale: the existing lender may call the whole loan due when title transfers. Federal law (Garn-St Germain) generally lets it do so, and the transfer exemptions do not cover a sale to an unrelated investor. Have a written plan, and the money, to refinance or pay off the loan if that happens.
Never misrepresent ownership, occupancy or who is paying to a lender or an insurer. That can be mortgage or insurance fraud.

Foreclosure rescue and equity purchaser laws: if the seller is behind on payments or in foreclosure, many states impose strict contract language, cancellation rights and prohibitions on buyers. Examples include California Civil Code §1695 et seq., New York Real Property Law §265-a, Maryland, Illinois and Minnesota. Violations can void the deal and create criminal liability.

Texas: Property Code §5.016 requires a separate seller notice to the buyer and each lienholder at least seven days before contracting or conveying when a lien stays on residential property, unless an exception applies.
The seller should get independent legal advice. A buyer's attorney or title company does not represent the seller.
The seller stays legally liable on the loan. Late payments by the buyer hurt the seller's credit, and a foreclosure can lead to a deficiency claim against the seller where state law allows.
Insurance is a common failure point. Make sure the property is properly insured for the actual owner and occupancy, the lender stays listed as mortgagee, and nobody misstates facts to the insurer.
A limited power of attorney must follow your state's execution rules, often notarization, and should never authorize new borrowing in the seller's name.
Escrow shortages, tax reassessments after sale and HOA transfer fees can raise the monthly payment. Budget for them.
VA loans: the seller's VA entitlement generally stays tied up while the loan is outstanding unless a qualified veteran substitutes entitlement.

sections.title: 1. What this addendum does
sections.body:
This addendum, dated {{addendum_date}}, is part of the purchase contract dated {{contract_date}} between {{buyer_name}} ("Buyer") and {{seller_name}} ("Seller") for {{property_address}}, {{state}} (the "Property"). If it conflicts with the purchase contract, this addendum controls.

**In plain terms:** Seller will deed the Property to Buyer. Seller's existing mortgage will stay in Seller's name and will not be paid off at closing. Buyer will make the mortgage payments from now on. The lender has not agreed to this and may have the right to demand full payment.

sections.title: 2. Existing loans
sections.body:
The Property is subject to these loans (the "Existing Loans"):

- **First loan:** {{loan1_lender}}, loan ending in {{loan1_last4}}, approximate balance {{loan1_balance}}, rate {{loan1_rate}}%, monthly payment {{loan1_payment}} ({{loan1_type}}).

sections.title: 3. Loan escrow account
sections.body: The first loan has an escrow account for property taxes and insurance. The monthly payment includes escrow and can change after each annual escrow analysis, for example because of a tax reassessment after the sale or a new insurance premium. Buyer pays any escrow shortage or increased payment. Buyer: [[initial:buyer]]

sections.title: 4. Second loan
sections.body: - **Second loan:** {{loan2_details}}

sections.title: 5. Purchase subject to the Existing Loans
sections.body: Buyer takes title subject to the Existing Loans. Buyer does not assume them, and the lender has not released Seller. The approximate balances are credited toward the purchase price as stated in the purchase contract. The actual balances may differ from the estimates. Buyer has received copies of the most recent loan statements. Buyer: [[initial:buyer]]

sections.title: 6. Seller acknowledgments
sections.body:
Seller understands and agrees, initialing each statement:

- The Existing Loans stay in my name. I remain legally responsible to the lender until they are paid off or the lender releases me in writing. Initials: [[initial:seller]]
- I will no longer own the Property, but loan payments, late payments, defaults and any foreclosure will continue to be reported on my credit. Initials: [[initial:seller]]
- The lender may call the loan due because of this sale (see the Due-on-sale section). If Buyer cannot pay it off, the Property could be foreclosed and my credit harmed. Initials: [[initial:seller]]
- The Existing Loans will continue to count as my debt, which may affect my ability to get new credit, including a mortgage on another home. Initials: [[initial:seller]]
- I will keep receiving tax forms for the loan, such as Form 1098 mortgage interest statements, and I should get tax advice about this sale and who may deduct mortgage interest. Initials: [[initial:seller]]
- I was advised to have my own attorney review this transaction, and I had the opportunity to do so. Initials: [[initial:seller]]

sections.title: 7. Buyer acknowledgments
sections.body:
Buyer understands and agrees, initialing each statement:

- I will make every payment on the Existing Loans in full and on time, starting with the payment due {{first_buyer_payment}}, until they are paid off or refinanced. Initials: [[initial:buyer]]
- The lender may call the loan due. I am responsible for paying it off, refinancing or otherwise resolving it under the plan below, and I have, or have a realistic way to obtain, the money to do that. Initials: [[initial:buyer]]
- Payment amounts can change, for example because of escrow shortages, tax reassessment after the sale, insurance increases or an adjustable rate. I am responsible for the full amount due. Initials: [[initial:buyer]]
- I will not represent myself to the lender or any insurer as the borrower, or misstate who owns or occupies the Property. Initials: [[initial:buyer]]

sections.title: 8. Due-on-sale
sections.body:
Most residential mortgages contain a "due-on-sale" clause. Federal law (the Garn-St Germain Act, 12 U.S.C. §1701j-3) generally allows the lender to enforce it and demand payment of the entire loan balance when the property, or an interest in it, is transferred without the lender's consent. Transfers to an unrelated buyer, including through a land trust where the buyer becomes a beneficiary, generally are not within the Act's exemptions. Leases longer than three years, or any lease with an option to purchase, are not exempt either.

Neither party has made any promise that the lender will not call the loan due. Buyer: [[initial:buyer]] Seller: [[initial:seller]]

sections.title: 9. If the lender calls the loan: refinance, pay off or sell
sections.body: If the lender demands payment in full, Buyer will, at Buyer's sole expense and before the lender's deadline (or any extension the lender grants), refinance or pay off the Existing Loans, sell the Property and pay them off, or negotiate an assumption or other resolution the lender accepts in writing that releases or protects Seller. Buyer will keep making regular payments in the meantime, if the lender accepts them.
sections.showIf: acceleration_plan == 'refinance, pay off or sell before the lender deadline'

sections.title: 10. If the lender calls the loan: refinance, pay off, sell or deed back
sections.body: If the lender demands payment in full, Buyer will, at Buyer's sole expense and before the lender's deadline (or any extension the lender grants), refinance or pay off the Existing Loans, sell the Property and pay them off, or negotiate an assumption or other resolution the lender accepts in writing. If Buyer cannot do any of these at least 30 days before the lender's deadline, Buyer will, at Seller's written election, convey the Property back to Seller by deed free of any liens or encumbrances Buyer created, with the loans current. Buyer will not be entitled to a refund of amounts paid. **The parties understand that a court may review a deed-back for fairness, and that state law may require a different process.** Buyer: [[initial:buyer]] Seller: [[initial:seller]]
sections.showIf: acceleration_plan == 'refinance, pay off or sell, or deed the property back to seller'

sections.title: 11. Payments and proof
sections.body: Buyer will make payments {{payment_method}}. Servicing company (if any): {{servicer_name}}. Within {{proof_days}} days after each due date, Buyer will give Seller proof that the payment was made, or Seller will have access to the servicer's payment records. Seller may contact the lender at any time to confirm loan status.

sections.title: 12. Missed payments
sections.body: If a payment is not made by its due date (including the lender's grace period), Seller may give Buyer written notice. If Buyer does not make the payment, with any late fees, within {{cure_days}} days after notice, Buyer is in default. Seller may then make the payment, and Buyer will repay Seller within 10 days with interest at the highest lawful rate or 10% per year, whichever is lower. Seller may also pursue any other remedy the law and this agreement allow. Buyer's obligations under this addendum survive closing.

sections.title: 13. Security for Buyer's promises
sections.body: To secure Buyer's obligation to keep the Existing Loans current and to repay any amounts Seller advances, Buyer will sign at closing a deed of trust or mortgage on the Property in favor of Seller, junior to the Existing Loans, drafted by an attorney to comply with the law of {{state}} and recorded in the county records. On a default, Seller may foreclose it as that law permits.

sections.title: 14. Past-due amounts and escrow
sections.body: Past-due amounts on the Existing Loans at signing: {{arrears}}, to be paid by {{arrears_paid_by}}, so the loans are current at closing. The existing loan escrow account balance goes to {{escrow_balance}}. Any later escrow refund from the lender that belongs to Buyer will be paid to Buyer by Seller within 10 days after Seller receives it.

sections.title: 15. Insurance
sections.body: Insurance plan: {{insurance_plan}}. From closing, Buyer will keep the Property insured for its full replacement cost (plus flood insurance if the lender requires it), with the existing lender named as mortgagee as the loan documents require. Seller will be added as an additional insured or additional interest where the insurer allows. Each party will give the insurer accurate information about ownership and occupancy. Buyer will give Seller proof of coverage at closing and at each renewal. If the lender force-places insurance, Buyer will pay its cost and promptly obtain compliant coverage.

sections.title: 16. Authorization and limited power of attorney
17. Title, taxes and association
sections.body: Seller will convey title by the deed specified in the purchase contract, and the deed will be recorded. Buyer will obtain an owner's title insurance policy if available. From closing, Buyer pays property taxes, association dues, utilities and maintenance, whether or not escrowed. Seller will give Buyer copies of loan, tax, insurance and association notices Seller receives, within 5 days.

sections.title: 18. Payoff target
sections.body: Buyer intends to pay off or refinance the Existing Loans within {{payoff_years}} years, if a target is stated. Buyer will in any case pay them off when Buyer sells or transfers the Property. Buyer will not further encumber the Property in a way that impairs the Existing Loans.

sections.title: 19. Texas: notice of existing lien (Prop. Code §5.016)
sections.body: **Texas.** If the property is residential and an existing recorded lien will remain after the sale, Texas Property Code §5.016 requires the seller to give the buyer, and each lienholder, a separate written notice in at least 12-point type. It must be given at least seven days before the earlier of signing a binding contract or conveying the property, and it must contain the statutory warning and loan details. If a contract was signed without the notice, the buyer may terminate it within seven days after receiving the notice. Exceptions exist, for example when the buyer obtains a title insurance policy, or the buyer has bought, sold or contracted for four or more properties in the previous 12 months. The parties confirm that they have determined whether §5.016 applies and, if it does, that the notice was given on: {{tx_notice_date}}. Seller: [[initial:seller]] Buyer: [[initial:buyer]]

sections.title: 20. Seller in default or foreclosure
sections.body: If the Existing Loans were in default, or any foreclosure notice had been issued, when the parties first discussed this transaction, the parties confirm they have checked whether the foreclosure-rescue or equity-purchaser law of {{state}} applies, and have complied with any required contract language, notices and cancellation rights. Buyer: [[initial:buyer]] Seller: [[initial:seller]]

sections.title: 21. State-specific requirements
sections.body: The property is in {{state}}. The parties will comply with that state's requirements for this transaction, including required seller disclosures and forms, licensing rules, closing and recording requirements, and any mandatory statutory notices. Massless shows a summary of known requirements for {{state}} with this template. That summary is a starting point, may be incomplete or out of date, and is not part of this agreement. Any addendum or disclosure form the state requires will be attached and signed by the parties.

sections.title: 22. Independent advice
sections.body: Each party has had the opportunity to consult its own attorney and tax adviser, and is not relying on the other party for legal, tax or financial advice. The closing agent does not represent Seller or Buyer unless separately engaged.

sections.title: Signatures
sections.body:
By signing below, each party agrees to this document.

**Buyer** — {{buyer_name}}

[[sig:buyer]]

Printed name: [[name:buyer]]
Date: [[date:buyer]]

**Seller** — {{seller_name}}

[[sig:seller]]

Printed name: [[name:seller]]
Date: [[date:seller]]

disclaimer: This is a starting template from the Massless open contract library. It is not legal advice, and using it does not create an attorney-client relationship. Laws vary by state and change over time. Have a licensed attorney in your state review it before you sign. Real estate contracts carry state-specific disclosure, licensing, closing and recording rules. If a real estate licensee is involved, the licensee may be required to use state-promulgated or approved forms instead of this one (for example in Texas and Colorado). Deeds, mortgages and deeds of trust usually must be notarized and recorded; an electronic signature on this document does not record anything. Creative-finance transactions (subject-to, seller financing, wraps, lease-options, contracts for deed) can trigger lender due-on-sale rights, federal and state lending and licensing laws (Truth in Lending/Dodd-Frank, SAFE Act), state executory-contract statutes and consumer-protection claims. Each party, and especially the seller, should have independent legal counsel and a tax adviser before signing.
